The fix is one service in front, and it is cheaper per gigabyte, it caches so most requests never reach the bucket at all, and the traffic from the bucket to it is not charged. That is the shape of this whole domain.
Domain four, design cost optimised architectures. Twenty percent, and the smallest domain on the paper.
Which sounds like the one to skip.
It is the one people skip and then lose marks in the other three domains, because cost is the qualifier that separates two correct answers everywhere else.
And this is the only domain where the right answer is allowed to be worse. Slower retrieval, an interruptible machine, one availability zone instead of three.
So the question is what am I allowed to give up.
What am I allowed to give up, and the stem always tells you. Three levers. What you commit to, where the data sits, and how much of it moves.
Lever one, commitment. Four ways to buy compute, and the exam expects you to layer them rather than choose one.
On demand is the default. No commitment, highest rate, and it is the right answer for genuinely unpredictable work and for short lived spikes.

A savings plan is a commitment to spend a certain amount per hour for one or three years, in exchange for a large discount. The flexible variety applies across instance families, regions, and to containers and functions as well.
And reserved instances, which is the older idea?

A commitment to a particular configuration rather than to an amount of spend. Still on the exam, and still the answer when the question stresses a specific instance type in a specific zone, or a capacity reservation.
For everything steady, the modern answer is the savings plan, because it survives changing your mind about instance types.
Then the interesting one. Spare capacity, sold at a very large discount, up to about ninety percent, and reclaimed with about two minutes of warning when it is needed elsewhere.
Which sounds unusable for anything real.

It is unusable for anything that cannot be interrupted, and perfect for anything that can. Batch rendering, data processing, test suites, stateless workers behind a queue. If the stem says fault tolerant, or can be restarted, that word is there on purpose.
Lever two, tiering. Object storage classes, and the exam tests the conditions rather than the names.
Standard for frequent access. Infrequent access for data you still need immediately but rarely, cheaper to store and charged when you retrieve it, with a thirty day minimum.
The single zone version is cheaper again, and it is only ever correct when losing the data would be an inconvenience rather than a disaster. Copies of something reproducible.
And the archive tiers, where retrieval takes time.

Three of them. One retrieves in milliseconds but has a ninety day minimum. One retrieves in minutes to hours. And the deepest is the cheapest storage available with a retrieval measured in hours and a one hundred and eighty day minimum.
That minimum duration is the trap. Deleting early still charges you for the full minimum, so archiving something you will delete next month costs more, not less.

And when the access pattern is genuinely unknown or changing, the tier that moves objects automatically is the answer. It charges a small monitoring fee per object and no retrieval fee, and it is the correct answer to the phrase unpredictable access.
Now a scenario. One platform, three workloads. A steady set of web servers running all year. A nightly analytics job that takes four hours. And a development environment used nine to five, weekdays.
Reserved capacity for all three. Commit to everything and take the discount.
It is defensible and it is what a lot of teams do. Walk me through the analytics job on that plan.
Four hours a night, so I am committed twenty four hours a day and using four. I am paying for twenty hours of nothing to get a discount on four.

And the job restarts safely if it dies, which is the word that unlocks the discount you actually want. Interruptible capacity, up to ninety percent off, and the four hours cost less than the commitment would have.
Fine. And the development environment?

Nine to five on weekdays is forty hours out of a hundred and sixty eight. So the lever is not the purchase model at all. It is a schedule that stops the instances at night and starts them in the morning.
Scheduled scaling is a cost answer, not a performance one, and it appears in this domain regularly. Roughly three quarters of the bill for that environment is hours nobody was working.
So only the web servers deserve a commitment.

Only the steady baseline. And even there, commit to the baseline rather than the peak, and let the peak run on demand. Over committing is a real trap because the commitment does not shrink when your traffic does.
Now lever three, and this is where the cold open lives. Movement. Data coming in is free. Data going out to the internet is charged by the gigabyte.
What about inside the region? Between zones.
Charged, in both directions, and this one surprises people. A chatty set of services spread across three zones for resilience is paying for that resilience on every internal call.
Which is not an argument against multiple zones. It is an argument for noticing. And two specific fixes come up constantly. A delivery network in front of anything served repeatedly to the internet.

And an endpoint for object storage so private machines stop pulling their data through a gateway that charges by the gigabyte. That one appeared in the security domain as well, which is unusual and worth remembering.

Commit for the steady baseline with a savings plan. Reserved capacity when the question insists on a specific configuration or a reservation. Interruptible capacity for anything the stem calls fault tolerant. On demand for the spike on top.
Before buying anything, turn it off when nobody is using it. A schedule is the cheapest saving available and it needs no commitment.
Tier storage by how soon you need it and how bad losing it would be. Watch the minimum durations, because early deletion is charged as if you had kept it.
Unknown or changing access is the automatic tiering class. Reproducible copies are the single zone class. Everything else follows the retrieval time you can live with.
And watch what moves. Out to the internet is charged. Between zones is charged in both directions. A delivery network and a storage endpoint remove two of the biggest transfer lines that exist.
Same files, sent again and again, at full price. The service in front cached most of them and the traffic from the bucket to that service was not charged at all.
Drill. Question one. A nightly batch job of four hours restarts cleanly if it fails. Which purchase model, and what word in the stem told you?
Interruptible spare capacity. The word is restarts, or fault tolerant. It is the phrase that unlocks the deepest discount.
Question two. Logs must be kept seven years for an audit and will almost certainly never be read. Which class, and what is the risk?
The deepest archive tier. The risk is retrieval time in hours, and a minimum storage duration of a hundred and eighty days if anything is deleted early.
Question three. Access patterns are unknown and change month to month. Which class, and why not infrequent access?
The automatic tiering class. Infrequent access charges a retrieval fee, which punishes you when the data turns out to be popular after all.
Question four. A development environment is used forty hours a week. What is the first thing you change?
Stop it outside those hours on a schedule. No commitment beats paying a discounted rate for a hundred and twenty idle hours.
Three traps and their mechanisms.

Trap one is the commitment offered for variable work. It is on the screen because commitments genuinely save money, and it is wrong whenever the workload is spiky, temporary, or about to be re-architected.
The tell being any mention of change.
Migrating, piloting, seasonal, or being retired next year. All of those rule out a one or three year commitment, no matter how attractive the discount is.

Trap two is the cheap storage tier applied to data that cannot be lost or is needed quickly. The single zone class and the deep archive class are both correct answers to narrow questions and expensive mistakes everywhere else.
Read for two things. Can this data be regenerated, and how fast must it come back. Those decide the class before price does.
Trap three is optimising the wrong line. The instance is visible, so people size it. The transfer charge is invisible, so nobody looks at it.
And on a content heavy platform it is the biggest number on the bill.
Which is why a question that describes a surprising bill on a read heavy public workload is almost never asking about instance size. It is asking what is moving, and how often.
Three questions for yourself.
One. What am I allowed to give up here, and which word in the stem gave me permission?
Two. What is the minimum duration charge, and would deleting early cost me more than keeping it?
Three. What is actually moving, and is anyone paying for it twice?
And the cheapest optimisation of all.
Turning it off. Before any purchase model, before any tier, ask whether it needed to be running at all.
Marks per hour: the highest per page of study on the exam. The domain is small, the rules are short, and the same rules break ties in the other three domains.
That is all four domains covered. Secure, resilient, high performing, cost optimised, and the two service discriminator episodes still to come.
Before those, do the thing that actually moves the score. Sit an official practice exam, and only book the real one once you are consistently over eighty percent on it.

c: Why this sits across two domains
l: This is not a domain episode. It is a depth episode, and it sits across two of them. Domain three, applications of foundation models, is twenty eight percent and names prompt engineering techniques and inference parameters directly. Domain five, security and governance, is fourteen percent and names prompt attacks.

Together that is a large slice of the paper, and it is a slice where the questions are unusually concrete. Not which approach do you choose, but what does this specific setting do, and what is this specific attack called.

So the standard the examiner holds you to here is naming. You need the names of four prompt techniques, four inference settings, and three attacks, and you need to know what each one changes. That is the episode.

Start with the anatomy of a prompt, because the exam uses these words as if you know them. A well formed prompt has an instruction, some context, the input itself, and an indication of the output you expect. Missing the last one is why models answer in a shape you did not want.

Now the techniques, by name. Zero shot is asking with no examples. Few shot is including a handful of worked examples so the model infers the pattern from them. That difference is simply whether examples are present, and questions do test it that plainly.

Chain of thought is asking the model to reason step by step before answering. It helps measurably on multi step problems, arithmetic and logic, and it costs more tokens and more time. When a question describes a model getting the right pieces but the wrong final answer, chain of thought is the technique being pointed at.

A prompt template is the fourth term. It is a reusable prompt with placeholders, so the same structure serves many inputs. When a question describes inconsistent results across a team all writing their own prompts, the answer is a shared template, not a different model.

Now the inference settings, and this is where marks are won because most people learn only one of them. Temperature controls randomness. Low temperature makes the model pick the likely words, so output is more deterministic and more repeatable. High temperature makes it more varied and more creative.

So a requirement for consistent, reproducible, factual output means lower the temperature. A requirement for varied marketing copy or brainstorming means raise it. That mapping alone answers several questions.

Top p and top k are the other two, and they do something related but different. They limit which words the model may choose from at all. Top k keeps the k most likely candidates. Top p keeps the smallest set of candidates whose probabilities add up to p.

The useful way to hold it: temperature reshapes the odds, top p and top k cut the shortlist. All three reduce or increase variety, and the exam will not ask you to tune them precisely. It will ask which direction to move for a stated outcome.

Two more settings. Maximum length, or maximum tokens, caps how long a response may be. It controls cost and truncation, and it does nothing whatsoever for quality. Stop sequences tell the model to stop when it produces a particular string, which is how you keep it from rambling past the answer.

And one limit that ties the whole thing together. The context window is the total amount of text the model can consider at once, prompt and response together. Few shot examples, retrieved documents and conversation history all consume it. When a question describes a chat assistant that forgets earlier turns, that is the context window, not a fault.

Cost and latency both follow tokens. More input tokens and more output tokens mean more money and more waiting. That is why a long few shot prompt sent millions of times is a real design decision and not a free improvement.

On AWS, all of this lives in Amazon Bedrock. The inference settings are parameters on the Bedrock inference call, and the same settings appear in the playground where you experiment before writing code.

Bedrock prompt management is where reusable prompt templates are stored and versioned, so the same prompt is not pasted into six applications. If a question asks how to standardise prompts across teams, that is the capability being described.

Bedrock Guardrails is the control layer, and this is the one to know cold. It applies content filters, denied topics, word filters and sensitive information filtering, and it applies them to the prompt going in and to the response coming out, independently of any model.
That independence is the point. A guardrail is configuration outside the model. An instruction in the prompt is text inside the model's input, competing with whatever else arrived in that input.

Now the three attacks, because they are named in the exam guide and they are easy marks once separated. Prompt injection is content that arrives as data and is treated as instructions. A document, a support ticket, a web page. The model cannot tell the difference between your instructions and the attacker's.

Jailbreaking is the user themselves working around the safety rules, usually by roleplay or by pretending the rules do not apply. The difference from injection is who is doing it and where the text comes from. Injection arrives inside content. Jailbreaking comes from the person typing.

Poisoning is different again and happens earlier. It is corrupting the training or the fine tuning data so the model itself behaves badly afterwards. If the question describes bad data going into training, it is poisoning. If it describes bad text going into a prompt, it is injection.

The defence for the first two is Guardrails plus least privilege on whatever the model is allowed to do. The defence for poisoning is data provenance and validation before training, which is a data governance answer, not a prompting one.

Trap one. Temperature offered as a fix for accuracy. Lowering temperature makes output more consistent and more predictable. It does not make the model know more. If a question is about wrong facts, the answer is retrieval or grounding, not a parameter.

Trap two. Maximum tokens offered as a quality control. Raising the limit lets an answer be longer. It never makes an answer better, and lowering it truncates rather than summarises. Any option that treats the length cap as a quality dial is a distractor.

Trap three. Few shot examples confused with fine tuning. Few shot means examples in the prompt, right now, for this one request, at token cost every time. Fine tuning means training the model on examples once, permanently. If the stem says the examples must be provided with every request, it is few shot by definition.

Trap four, and it is the one people lose. A prompt instruction offered as a security control. An option that says instruct the model to refuse harmful requests looks responsible and is not the security answer, because the attacker's text arrives through the same channel.

The security answers sit outside the model. A configured guardrail, and narrow permissions on whatever the model can call. Remember the shape: guardrails reduce the chance, permissions reduce the damage.

Trap five. Injection and jailbreaking used interchangeably. They are separate terms in the exam guide. Ask where the malicious text came from. From content the system ingested, injection. From the user in the conversation, jailbreaking.
Recall drill. Question one. A support summary must come out the same way every time for the same input. Which setting do you change, and in which direction?
Temperature, lowered. Low temperature favours likely words and makes output more deterministic and repeatable.
Question two. A chat assistant stops referring to things the user said earlier in a long conversation. What is happening?
The context window is full. Prompt, history and response share one budget, and the earliest turns fall out of it.
Question three. A customer pastes text into a form and the assistant follows it as an instruction. Name the attack, and name the two controls.
Prompt injection. Guardrails filtering input and output, and least privilege on what the application is permitted to do.
Question four. Accuracy on a multi step reasoning task is poor, there is no budget and no training data. What do you try?
Chain of thought prompting, and a few worked examples. Both cost tokens only, and both are the cheapest step on the ladder.
Question five. Someone corrupted the fine tuning dataset. Is that injection, jailbreaking, or poisoning?
Poisoning. It happens to the data before training. Injection and jailbreaking both happen at inference time.
Three things to carry in. Temperature reshapes the odds, top p and top k cut the shortlist, and maximum length only truncates. None of the three makes a model more correct.
Injection arrives in content, jailbreaking comes from the user, poisoning happens to the training data. Where did the bad text come from is the whole question.
And the sentence worth memorising verbatim. Guardrails reduce the chance, permissions reduce the damage, and an instruction in the prompt is not a control.
Next: choosing between models in the first place, and proving the one you chose is working. Which is where the metrics with strange names live.
You applied for a job in Sydney that pays up to a hundred and eighty thousand dollars.
The same job, at the same company, in the same city, is advertised at up to three hundred and sixty.
That cannot be the same job. Nobody publishes two bands that far apart.
They do when a company is mid-rebrand. One ad is the old company. One is the new one.
On Thursday at three you get thirty minutes to find out which of the two you are standing in.
And if the call ends without asking?
Then the cheaper ad wins by default, because it is the one you applied through.
This is The DeployCo Screen. One call on Thursday the twentieth of August, at three in the afternoon.
The company is the OpenAI Deployment Company. Everyone calls it DeployCo, and the website is deploy dot co.
Let me state the obvious position first, so you can knock it down.
A recruiter screen is a formality. She checks you are real, checks your visa, and passes you on.
That is true at a large company with a fixed pipeline. It is not true here, and it is not true of this recruiter.
The real decision she makes is not pass or fail. It is which requisition and which level you get routed to.
Routing decides the money, the interviewers, and the whole shape of the loop after this.
So the win condition is not impressing her. It is being filed correctly.
Being filed correctly, and being memorable enough that she argues for you when the file is thin.
Three concepts carry this whole episode. First: she is a router, not an examiner.
Isabelle Atack is Member of Recruiting Staff at DeployCo, based in Sydney.
She joined Tomoro in April as Talent Acquisition Manager. Tomoro became DeployCo in July, and her title changed with it.
Before that she spent sixteen months at a London recruitment agency called Saragossa. Her degree is in English.
So she cannot judge whether the architecture was any good.
Correct, and that is the second concept. She is not judging the engineering. She is judging the translation.
The ad says the technical team is front of house. It asks for client ambassadors who explain complex ideas in an accessible manner.
She is exactly qualified to score that, because she is the accessible-manner test walking around on two legs.
Then the deep technical answer is wasted on her.
Worse than wasted. A deep technical answer to a non-technical listener reads as poor judgement about audience.
Third concept: the requisition. A requisition is the internal job record that carries the band and the level.
Two of them exist for this role, and you applied through the older, cheaper one.
Here is how the thirty minutes will actually run. It is the same shape at almost every company.
Minutes zero to three: she introduces herself and DeployCo, and asks if you can hear her.
Minutes three to ten: tell me about yourself. This is the single highest-leverage block in the call.
Seven minutes for a background walk seems generous.
It is not seven minutes of you talking. It is ninety seconds of you, then her questions inside your answer.
Minutes ten to eighteen: motivation. Why this role, why leave where you are, why customer-facing work.
Minutes eighteen to twenty-four: logistics and money. Notice period, work rights, location, travel, expectations.
Minutes twenty-four to thirty: your questions, and what happens next.
So the money conversation lands with six minutes left and no room to recover.
Yes, and that is precisely why the requisition question goes in earlier. You raise it, not her.
The natural place is the moment she describes the role. That is an invitation, and you take it.
Five numbers matter on Thursday, and every one of them is public.
One hundred and thirty thousand to a hundred and eighty thousand. That is the Tomoro ad you applied through.
It was published in September twenty twenty-five and has never been refreshed.
One hundred and thirty-five thousand to three hundred and sixty thousand, plus equity. That is the DeployCo Sydney ad.
It went live on the seventh of August this year, four days before you applied to the other one.
Then the wide band is just a range covering several levels. The top is not real for him.
Agreed, the top is not the target. But the midpoint of that band is about two hundred and forty-seven thousand.
And the body of that ad opens by saying they are seeking a senior applied AI software engineer.
Your floor is a hundred and eighty. The old ad tops out exactly at your floor.
So the old ad cannot pay him anything above the minimum he will accept.
That is the whole problem in one sentence. Say it to yourself before the call.
Now the whole thing in one continuous pass, with nothing new added.
She calls at three. You answer, sound pleased, and let her talk first.
She describes DeployCo and the Australian team. You listen for which role she names.
She asks about your background. You give the ninety-second version and stop talking.
She asks why this, and why now. You separate customer-facing work from pure engineering, out loud.
Somewhere in there she describes the role. That is your moment. You ask which requisition it is.
She answers, and now the salary conversation has a frame before any number is spoken.
She asks logistics. Sydney, four weeks notice, permanent resident, comfortable on client sites three days a week.
She asks expectations. You give a range tied to the scope in the ad, and you ask about the equity.
You ask two or three real questions. You ask what happens next and by when.
You thank her by name. The call ends. You write down what she said about the requisition.
Three failure modes, each with an early signal you can hear while it is happening.
First: answering the technical question technically. You say retrieval, orchestration, shadow mode, and she goes quiet.
The early signal is her follow-up getting shorter. Short follow-ups mean she has stopped tracking.

Then it meets reality, and it fails in four specific ways. Not vaguely. Four.

One. The process dies forty seconds into a two minute run. There is no resume point, because the only record of where you were is the call stack, and the call stack is gone. You start again from the top and pay for every token a second time.

Two. A human has to approve something before it happens. Sending the email, issuing the refund, merging the branch. In a loop, waiting for a human means holding a process open for however long that takes. Minutes is awkward. Hours is a leak. Days is impossible.

Three. Something goes wrong and you want to know which step made the bad call. Inside a loop, the decision was an if statement three frames deep. There is nothing to inspect afterwards. You have logs, if you remembered to write them.

Four. You need a rule that always holds. Never spend more than ten dollars. Never send without approval. In a loop where the model decides what happens next, that rule lives in the prompt, and a prompt is a suggestion.
LangGraph is what you get when you take those four problems seriously. It is not a smarter agent. It is the same agent, made resumable, pausable, inspectable, and constrained.
The whole framework is four declarations and one compile step.

First, a state schema. This is the part people underestimate, and it is the part that decides whether the rest works. You declare a typed dictionary whose keys are the things your agent knows. Messages. The current plan. A retry count. Whatever the run needs to carry.

That schema is not a convenience. It is the contract with the runtime. Anything in it gets persisted at every step and survives a crash. Anything not in it lives in a local variable and disappears the moment the process does.

Second, nodes. A node is a function that takes the state and returns a partial update. Not the whole state. Just the keys it touched. If a node classifies an email, it returns one key, the label. Everything else it leaves alone.

Third, edges. An edge says what runs next. Some edges are fixed: after classify, always draft. Some are conditional: you write an ordinary Python function that looks at the state and returns the name of the next node. That function is plain code. No model call. It is deterministic, and you can unit test it with a hand built dictionary in about four lines.

This is the moment the framework earns its keep, so sit with it. In the loop version, the model decides what happens next. In the graph version, your routing function decides, and the model only decides what goes into the state that your function reads. Control flow moved from the prompt into code.

Fourth, compile. The builder is validated and turned into a runnable object. Missing edge targets, unreachable nodes, no path to the end: those become errors at compile time rather than hangs at three in the morning.

Now, the part that surprises people. The engine underneath is not a for loop over nodes. It is a bulk synchronous parallel engine, the same model as Pregel, the graph processing system Google published for computing over very large graphs.

Execution advances in what the documentation calls super steps. In each super step, every node that has input runs. They all run against the same snapshot of the state. Then, and only then, all their updates are applied at once. Then the next set of nodes is scheduled.

That has one consequence you need to internalise before you write anything real. Two nodes running in the same super step cannot see each other's writes. If node B needs node A's output, they must be in different super steps. You express that by putting an edge between them. People spend an afternoon debugging this before they read it, and about four seconds after.

It has a second consequence. Because all the updates land together, two parallel branches might both write the same key. What happens then? That is what a reducer is for. A reducer is a function that says how a new value merges with the old one. No reducer means overwrite, last write wins. Add a reducer, and two branches writing a list get their lists concatenated instead of one silently winning.

The message history has its own reducer, because concatenating messages is not quite right. It merges by message identifier, so a message that is re emitted updates in place rather than appearing twice.

And then, one line: attach a checkpointer. Now the state after every super step is written to storage, keyed by a thread identifier. That single addition is what turns the graph from a function into a process. Conversation memory, crash recovery, the human pause, and the ability to rewind are all the same feature seen from four angles.
Let me be concrete about the defaults, because the numbers are where the design shows.

The recursion limit defaults to twenty five. That counts super steps, not node executions. So a fan out to fifty parallel nodes costs one step, while a thirty node chain costs thirty and trips the limit. It is a safety net against a routing bug that never terminates, not a budget dial. Raising it to fix a loop that does not stop converts a fast failure into an expensive one.

Durability is a choice you make per run, and there are three settings. Exit means state is written only when the run finishes. Fastest, and a crash halfway through loses everything. Async writes in the background after each step, which is the sensible default, with a small window where a crash costs you the last step. Sync writes before each step proceeds, which is the strongest guarantee and puts a database write on the critical path of every super step.

The rule for choosing is not about performance. It is about what a lost step costs. A research summariser can run on exit. Anything that spends money, calls a partner service, or waits on a human runs on sync.

For storage there is an in memory saver for tests, a SQLite saver for single node work, and a Postgres saver for production. The Postgres one needs a one time setup call to create its tables, and the first run fails on a missing table if you skip it.

One more real number. Checkpoints accumulate forever. There is no retention policy by default. Three months in, the checkpoint table is the largest object in the database, and nobody planned for it. That is the most common operational surprise in a LangGraph deployment, and it is a two line fix on day one and a migration later.
Now the honest part. This is real complexity, and there are cases where it is not worth it.
One model call with a fixed prompt does not need a graph. It needs a function. A straight line pipeline with no branching and no retry semantics does not need one either.

A tool calling agent with no approval step, no persistence requirement, and a short horizon is best served by the prebuilt agent, which is a single call that gives you the standard loop already compiled. It is still a graph underneath, so streaming and checkpointing work on it, but you did not write it.
The test I would apply is three words. Durability. Branching. Supervision. If none of those three is on your requirements list, a graph is ceremony.

There is a cost people miss too. The state schema is now a public contract. Adding a key is safe. Renaming one breaks any run that was in flight when you deployed, because it resumes into a state whose keys no longer match. You have to think about state migrations the way you think about database migrations, which is a discipline the loop never asked of you.

And there is a failure of adoption worth naming. People adopt LangGraph because they like the diagram, and then they write one enormous node with all the logic inside it. That node is the loop again, with extra imports. If your graph has three nodes and one of them is four hundred lines, you have not adopted anything.

The honest summary is this. A graph does not make an unreliable agent reliable. It makes an unreliable agent recoverable and observable, which is a different property and often the more valuable one. Per step accuracy still comes from your prompts, your tools, and your evaluations. Nothing about the topology fixes a bad tool description.
If this comes up in an interview, do not lead with the framework. Lead with the requirement.

Something like: the moment we needed an approval step before sending, we needed the run to survive the process, so state had to be persisted and the pause had to be a checkpoint rather than a blocked thread. That is what pushed us to a graph.

That sentence tells the interviewer you chose a tool for a reason rather than because it was on the front page. And if they push back and ask whether you could have done it with a queue and a database, the correct answer is yes, absolutely, and that is roughly what the framework is doing for you.
Next episode: state, channels, and reducers, which is where most of the real bugs live.
Here is a bug I want you to be able to diagnose in ten seconds by the end of this episode.
An agent runs. Each turn, the message history roughly doubles. By turn six the context window is full and the bill is absurd. Nothing in the code looks wrong. Every node does something reasonable.
And here is a second one. A node runs. The logs say it ran. It returns a value. The next node reads that value and sees the old one. No error. No warning. Just a stale read.

Both of those are state bugs, and both come from the same misunderstanding: that state in a graph works like a variable you assign to. It does not. It works like a set of channels, each with its own merge rule, updated in batches. Once you hold that model, both bugs are obvious.
This episode is about that model. It is the least glamorous part of the framework and by a wide margin the part that decides whether your agent works.
Start with the word channel, because it is the right word and dictionary is the wrong one.

Your state schema declares keys. Messages. Plan. Retry count. Each of those keys is an independent channel. It has a current value, and it has a rule for how a new value merges with the current one. Nodes do not assign to channels. Nodes emit updates, and the runtime applies them.

So a node returns a partial dictionary. Just the keys it touched. If a node bumps a retry counter, it returns one key with the new number, and every other channel is untouched. Not overwritten with the same value. Untouched.
That convention is what makes parallel branches possible at all. Two branches that write different keys can never conflict, because they are writing to different channels.
Now the merge rule. By default it is overwrite. Last write wins. For a scalar like the current plan, that is exactly right, and you should not change it.

But consider a channel that is a list, and two parallel branches that both append to it. With overwrite, one branch's work vanishes. In fact LangGraph will not let that happen quietly. Two writers to the same channel in the same step with no merge rule is an error, by design, rather than a silent choice of winner.

The fix is a reducer. You annotate the channel with a function that takes the current value and the update and returns the merged result. For a list of findings, that function is addition, which for lists means concatenation. Now both branches contribute and nothing is lost.

The message channel gets a specialised reducer, and it is worth knowing what it does beyond appending. It merges by message identifier. Same identifier, the message is replaced. New identifier, it is appended. That is what lets you edit or remove a message from history rather than only ever growing it.

So. Back to the doubling bug. If a node returns the entire message list rather than only the new messages, and the channel has an appending reducer, the runtime appends everything it was just given to what it already had. The list doubles. Every turn. The node looks completely reasonable in isolation, which is why this one costs people an afternoon.
The rule that prevents it: return your increment, never the whole channel.

Now the stale read. Remember that execution advances in super steps, and every node scheduled in a step runs against the same snapshot. If two nodes are in the same step, the second one cannot see the first one's write, because the writes have not been applied yet. They are applied together, at the end of the step.

So a stale read almost always means two nodes are running in parallel when you thought they were sequential. And the reason that happens is usually that someone added two edges out of one node expecting a choice, and got a fan out. Two unconditional edges out of a node is not pick one. It is run both.

One more state failure that is quieter than either. If your schema is a typed dictionary and a node returns a key that is not in the schema, that key is dropped. No error. The node ran, the update went nowhere, and the next node reads the previous value. A typo in a channel name is invisible. If that bothers you, and it should, use a Pydantic model for the state instead and pay a small validation cost per step to get a real error.
One last piece of the state model, because it decides how you compose things later. A compiled graph can be a node inside another graph. When that happens, the two schemas meet in one of two ways.

Either they share channel names, and the child reads and writes the parent's state directly. That is the least code and the most coupling, because renaming a key in the parent silently breaks the child, and a key that means something slightly different in each graph is a bug no type checker will find.

Or the parent wraps the child in a small function that translates: take these parent keys, build the child's input, call it, map the result back. More code, fully decoupled, and the child is independently testable. That is the right shape at a team boundary or anywhere the child has its own release cycle.
The decision is the same one you make with any module boundary. The only difference is that here the shared thing is a persisted schema, so getting it wrong is a migration rather than a refactor.
Some specifics from the documentation that shape how you design a schema.

The state is serialised into a checkpoint at every super step, not once at the end. That is the single most important fact for deciding what goes in it. A five megabyte document parked in state is written to storage on every step of the run. Store an identifier and fetch it in the node; do not carry the payload.

You can declare separate input and output schemas from the internal one. That means scratch channels, retry counters, raw tool payloads, intermediate scores, do not have to be part of what callers see. Worth doing early, because trimming the public surface later is a breaking change.
The prebuilt messages state is a typed dictionary with one channel, messages, already annotated with the message reducer. Subclass it and add your own keys. Most graphs start exactly there.

And a detail that catches people writing their own reducers. A reducer runs once per update, not once per step. Five parallel writers to one channel call it five times, in an order that is not guaranteed. If your reducer is not associative, different runs give different answers, and it will look like flakiness rather than a design error.
The trade-offs here are mostly about how much you put in state, and there is a real tension.

Everything in state is durable, inspectable, and time travellable. That argues for putting a lot in it. Everything in state is also serialised on every step and forms a schema you now have to migrate. That argues for putting a little in it.

My working rule is: state holds what a resume needs, plus what a human debugging the run would want to see. Not intermediate scratch that the node can recompute. Not large payloads. Not anything with a live handle, like a database connection or an open file, because those do not serialise at all.

On reducers, the tension is different. It is tempting, once you learn what they are, to add one to every channel. Resist that. Most scalar channels genuinely want last write wins, and a schema where every key accumulates is a schema that only grows. Add a reducer when you have an actual parallel writer or an actual accumulation, not as insurance.

There is one more trade-off worth naming, between typed dictionaries and Pydantic models. Typed dictionaries are fast and give you no runtime enforcement, so a channel declared as an integer can hold a string if some node put one there. Pydantic validates the input to each node and gives you a real error at the point of the mistake, at the cost of validating on every step. For a graph with many nodes and a schema that several people edit, I would pay that cost. For a five node graph you wrote yesterday, probably not.
The thing to demonstrate here is not that you know what a reducer is. It is that you know why one exists.
The clean way to say it: because updates from parallel branches land together, the framework needs a defined merge per key, and refusing to guess is better than silently picking a winner.

If you want to go one level further, mention that this is the same constraint bulk synchronous parallel systems have had since Pregel, and that the reason nodes cannot see each other's writes within a step is the same reason the merge has to be explicit. That answer says you understand the engine, not just the API.
Next episode: checkpoints, threads, and the pause, which is where the framework starts doing something a loop genuinely cannot.
A customer is charged twice for the same refund. The logs show the refund node ran once. The support ticket says otherwise, and the bank agrees with the support ticket.

What happened is not a bug in anyone's business logic. It is a rule about how a paused graph resumes, and it is the single most common defect that reaches production in a human in the loop system. By the end of this episode you will know the rule and the one line placement that prevents it.

But start with what you are buying. One line of setup, a checkpointer, and you get four things that look unrelated and are actually the same feature. Conversation memory. Crash recovery. A pause that can last three days. And the ability to rewind a run to any earlier point and take a different path.
They are the same feature because they all rest on one mechanism: after every super step, the entire state is written to storage under a thread identifier.
Attach a checkpointer when you compile. From that moment, every call must carry a thread identifier in its config.

Same thread identifier, same conversation, state carried forward. New thread identifier, clean slate. That is the whole memory model, and it is worth pausing on how much it is not doing. There is no summarisation, no retrieval, no cleverness. It is the state, saved, keyed by a string.

Which means the string matters enormously. Attach a checkpointer and forget to pass a thread identifier, and it raises, which is fine. Pass a fresh random one on every request, and every request has amnesia. The code looks right. Memory just never works. That is a much worse failure than an exception.

And it is a security boundary. If the thread identifier comes from the client, a user can ask for someone else's conversation and get it. Derive it on the server from the authenticated session. Always.

Now the pause. There is a function called interrupt. You call it inside a node with a payload. The graph stops, checkpoints, and surfaces that payload to whoever called it. The process can now exit entirely. Nothing is being held open.

Later, and later can mean three days, you call the graph again with a resume command carrying the human's answer. Execution restarts, and this time the interrupt call returns that answer instead of stopping.
Here is the rule. Resuming does not continue from the line after the interrupt. It re runs the node from the top. Everything before the interrupt call in that node executes a second time.

Read that again, because it is the refund bug. If your node charges the card and then asks for approval, the charge happens on the first pass, the graph pauses, the human approves, the node runs again from the top, and the card is charged again.

The fix is placement, not cleverness. Put the interrupt as early in the node as you can. Do the side effect after it, never before. If you cannot avoid work before the pause, put an idempotency key in state and check it at the top of the node.

There is a second flavour of the same idea called a static interrupt, configured at compile time: pause before this node, or after that one, without touching node code. Good for debugging, and good for a blanket policy like always approve sending. Less good for a conditional policy like only ask when the amount is over ten thousand, which is what the in node version gives you.

Then time travel, which falls out for free. Because every step is checkpointed, you can list the history of a thread, pick any checkpoint, and resume from it. Everything after that point re executes, and the new run branches off as its own line of history rather than overwriting the old one. So the original trajectory stays inspectable.

You can also edit state by hand, writing a new checkpoint as if a particular node had produced it. That is the fix the agent's mistake and let it carry on primitive. Note the as if a particular node part: which node you claim wrote it also determines what runs next, because routing is computed from the writing node. Get that argument wrong and your state edit is correct while the graph goes somewhere unexpected, which is a confusing thing to debug.
There is one more persistence layer, and confusing it with the checkpointer is a common mistake worth heading off.

The checkpointer remembers this conversation. A separate thing, called the store, remembers this user, across every conversation they ever have. They are deliberately different subsystems, because they have different jobs. Thread state is a transcript that has to replay exactly. Long term memory is a knowledge base that is written deliberately and read from everywhere.

The store is a namespaced key value store with optional semantic search. The namespace is a tuple, typically the user identifier and a category, and here is the part that matters: there is no implicit tenancy. Whatever you put in that namespace is the entire isolation model. Derive the first element from the authenticated session, never from model output, or you have built a cross tenant read.

And be selective about what goes in. Everything you retrieve from memory goes into the prompt and competes with the actual task for attention and budget. A store filled with restated conversation makes every future turn worse, not better. Stale memories are worse still, because a fact written eighteen months ago is now a confident falsehood the model has no reason to doubt.
Some specifics that matter when you build this.

A snapshot from the history is not just values. It carries the channel values, the nodes that are about to run, the checkpoint identifier, metadata about which node wrote it and at which step, and any pending tasks including interrupts. That is enough to reconstruct exactly why a run is where it is.

Multiple interrupt calls in one node are resolved positionally on resume. So if you reorder them between deploys, saved resume values match up with the wrong calls. Treat their order as part of your interface.

The documentation is explicit that a checkpointer and a thread identifier are required for interrupts. There is no pausing a stateless graph. If you want the human step, you have accepted the database.

Durability interacts with all of this. On the exit setting, state is written only when the run completes, so a crash mid run leaves nothing to resume. Anything that waits on a human runs on the synchronous setting, because the pause is precisely a crash you are choosing to have.
And replay does not undo side effects. Rewinding a run that sent emails sends the emails again on the way forward. Time travel is a debugging tool for state, not a transaction rollback.
What does this cost? Three things, and they are all operational rather than intellectual.

First, a database on the critical path. On the synchronous durability setting, every super step waits for a write. For a ten step graph, that is ten round trips you did not have before. The asynchronous setting gets most of the safety back for most of the speed, with a small window where a crash costs the last step.

Second, unbounded growth. Checkpoints accumulate and nothing removes them. A thread that lives for months holds every step of every turn. Decide retention on day one, when it is a configuration line, rather than in month four, when it is a migration against a table nobody wants to touch.

Third, schema coupling to in flight runs. A deploy that renames a channel breaks any run that was paused when it went out, because that run resumes into a state whose keys no longer match. Add channels freely. Renaming means draining first, or writing a migration.

And a design trade-off on the pause itself. A human approving a draft three days later is approving something written against a world that may have moved. The framework will happily resume; whether that is correct is your problem. Where the world can change, re validate after resume rather than trusting the paused state.
If someone asks how you would build an approval step, the weak answer describes a queue and a callback. The strong answer names the failure it prevents.

Try this. The pause has to be a checkpoint rather than a blocked thread, because a human might take days, and no process should be alive for that. And the node has to be written so that resuming re runs it from the top without repeating side effects, because that is what resume actually does.
That second sentence is the one that lands, because it is the thing people learn from an incident rather than from documentation.
Next episode: the last one, and the least glamorous. What actually breaks when this thing carries traffic.

The graph that works in a notebook and the graph that survives traffic differ in five places. Where state lives. Who owns the thread identifier. What happens when a step fails. What you can see afterwards. And what it costs.
None of those five is a feature you switch on. They are decisions, and the framework's contribution is that it makes them implementable rather than making them for you.
So this episode is a list of things that break, each with the decision that would have prevented it. Nothing here is exotic. All of it is boring, and all of it has happened.
Start with the failure that is easiest to cause and hardest to see coming: unbounded fan out.

There is a mechanism for dynamic parallelism. From a routing function you return a list of send objects, one per item, and each schedules an independent execution of a node with its own input. Twenty documents, twenty parallel summarisers. It is the map half of map reduce, and the reduce half is just a reducer on the channel they all write to.

It is also one line away from a live incident. Fan out over a query that returned two thousand rows and you launch two thousand model calls in a single super step. The runtime will do it. Your provider will not. The cap belongs in the routing function, before the fan out, and the number should be a constant someone chose rather than however many rows came back.

One subtlety about that mechanism, because it trips everyone once. The dictionary you send becomes the entire input to that node. Not a merge with the graph state. The whole input. So a node written against the full state, then reached by a send, fails on the first key it reads that you did not send. Give the mapped node its own narrow schema and the asymmetry becomes visible in the types instead of at runtime.

Next, retries. You can attach a retry policy per node, with attempts and backoff. Sensibly, the defaults retry on connection errors and transient server errors rather than on everything, and that instinct is correct: a parsing error in your own code will not improve on the third attempt, and retrying it just triples the latency of a guaranteed failure.

But a retried node re runs the whole node. Side effects included. So the same rule as the human pause applies here, for the same reason: idempotency is not a nice property, it is the precondition for every recovery mechanism in the system. Retry, resume, replay, and step re execution all mean the same thing to your node, which is that it may run twice.

That is worth stating as a ranking. If you can only do one thing for reliability, make nodes idempotent. It is worth more than the retry policy, more than the fallback, more than any of it, because everything else assumes it.

Second on that list is not more retries. It is fallback routing. After three failures, route to a smaller model, or a cached answer, or a human. That is a conditional edge, not a try block, and it is the thing that keeps the product usable during a provider outage rather than merely correct about being broken.

Then caching. You can cache a node on its input with a time to live. Worth it for deterministic expensive work that repeats. Not worth it for anything time sensitive. And be realistic about hit rates: a node whose input includes the whole message history has a different key every single turn, so the cache never hits and you have added a lookup for nothing. Cache narrow nodes with narrow inputs.

Last of the mechanics, streaming, which people file under user experience and is actually an operational tool. There are several granularities. Full state after each step, which is heavy. Just the deltas each node returned, which is what drives a progress display. Model tokens as they are generated. And a custom channel that a node can write to from inside itself.

That last one matters more than it sounds. The delta stream fires when a node finishes, which is exactly when the user has already decided your product is broken. If a node takes forty seconds, it has to report from inside, and the custom stream is the only way to do it.
The concrete operational facts, in the order they tend to bite.

One. The in memory checkpointer in production. It works in development and in a single instance staging environment, and it loses every conversation on deploy. The failure is silent because everything still functions; users just find their history gone.
Two. No checkpoint retention. Nothing prunes them. This shows up as an unexplained database bill and a table that is awkward to clean once it is large.

Three. Serverless and long runs. The function times out mid graph. On synchronous durability the run is resumable and you can pick it back up. On the exit setting it is simply gone, having spent every token along the way.

Four. Recursion limit raised to make an error go away. The default of twenty five counts super steps. When you hit it, the honest question is which cycle does not terminate, and raising the number converts a fast, cheap failure into a slow, expensive one.

Five. Cost measured per call. Retries are billed per attempt, and multi agent handoffs re read context, so the right unit is cost per completed run. A cheap model that fails twice and retries is more expensive than an expensive model that works, and per call metrics hide that completely.

And on observability, the pairing worth having is traces plus checkpoint history. Traces tell you what happened. The checkpoint history lets you rewind to the step before it happened and try again with one thing changed. Having both is the practical argument for running a graph rather than a loop, and it is worth more than any single feature in the framework.
The big deployment trade-off is one question: do you need runs that outlive an HTTP request?
If the answer is no, compile the graph and call it inside your own service. Total control, and you own scaling and queuing, which you were doing anyway.

If the answer is yes, you need a queue, a durable store, and something that can hand back a run identifier. You can build that, or you can run a server that provides threads, runs and streaming over HTTP with Postgres and Redis behind it, or you can pay for that server operated by someone else. The work is the same in all three cases. The only question is who does it.

On multi agent, which is the direction everyone drifts: it is a context isolation technique, not an intelligence multiplier. Splitting one agent into four gives each a smaller tool list and a narrower prompt. It also multiplies token spend, typically five to fifteen times for the same task, and adds a coordination failure that did not exist before. Two agents that can hand to each other will ping pong, and a hop counter with a hard cap in the router is not optional.

Build a subgraph when you want clean code. Build a second agent when a single agent's context or tool list has genuinely stopped working. Those are different problems and only one of them costs five times as much.

Testing is the cheapest thing on this list and the most skipped. Routing functions are pure functions over a dictionary, so they unit test in four lines and they cover most of your control flow. Then one graph level test with a fake model and an in memory checkpointer, asserting the sequence of nodes visited. And one resume test: interrupt, resume, assert the side effect happened once. That last test is the regression test for the duplicate charge, and it is about fifteen lines.
The move here is to answer an operational question operationally.

If someone asks how you would make an agent reliable, do not start with prompts. Start with: every recovery mechanism in the system re runs a node, so the first requirement is that nodes are idempotent. Then retries for the transient tail. Then a degraded path for sustained failure.
And if they ask what surprised you, the checkpoint table is a good answer, because it is specific, unglamorous, and clearly the answer of someone who ran the thing rather than read about it.

That closes the series. Four episodes: why a graph, state and reducers, checkpoints and the pause, and what breaks. If you take one sentence from all of it, take this one. The framework does not make your agent smarter. It makes it recoverable, inspectable, and constrained, and those three are what turn a demo into something you can leave running.
